facts.title: First day of Ramadan
facts.content: Muslims worldwide begin fasting at dawn (Fajr) and break at sunset (Maghrib). The pre-dawn meal is called Suhoor, and the sunset meal is Iftar.

facts.title: Lunar calendar
facts.content: Ramadan is the ninth month of the Islamic (Hijri) lunar calendar. Each month begins with the sighting of the new moon, so dates shift by about 11 days each solar year.

facts.title: Charity in Ramadan
facts.content: Zakat (obligatory charity) is often calculated and paid during Ramadan. Voluntary charity (sadaqah) is also highly encouraged—rewards are believed to be multiplied.

facts.title: Suhoor wisdom
facts.content: The Prophet (PBUH) said: 'Take suhoor, for in suhoor there is blessing.' Eating close to dawn helps sustain energy and reduces thirst during the day.

facts.title: Breaking with dates
facts.content: Breaking fast with dates and water follows the Prophet's practice. Dates provide quick energy and minerals after a long fast.

facts.title: Laylat al-Qadr
facts.content: The Night of Decree falls in the last ten nights of Ramadan. It commemorates the night the Quran was first revealed; worship on this night is better than a thousand months.

facts.title: Week one complete
facts.content: By day seven, many people adjust to the fasting rhythm. Staying hydrated between Iftar and Suhoor is key to feeling well.

facts.title: Taraweeh prayers
facts.content: Taraweeh are special voluntary night prayers performed during Ramadan. Many mosques hold them in congregation after the Isha prayer.

facts.title: Cultural diversity
facts.content: Ramadan is observed in every continent. Traditions vary—from cannon fire at Iftar in Egypt to street feasts in Indonesia—but the core of fasting unites Muslims globally.

facts.title: Health and fasting
facts.content: Intermittent fasting during Ramadan can support metabolic health. Always consult a doctor if you have medical conditions.

facts.title: Patience (Sabr)
facts.content: Ramadan is sometimes called the month of patience. Fasting teaches self-control, empathy, and gratitude.

facts.title: Eid preparation
facts.content: As Ramadan progresses, many prepare for Eid al-Fitr: the festival of breaking the fast, marked by prayer, family gatherings, and festive meals.

facts.title: White Days
facts.content: The 13th, 14th, and 15th of each Islamic month are the 'White Days.' Fasting on these days is a recommended Sunnah practice year-round.

facts.title: Halfway point
facts.content: Around the middle of Ramadan, focus often shifts to the last ten nights and Laylat al-Qadr. Many increase night worship and charity.

facts.title: Last fifteen nights
facts.content: The last fifteen nights are especially significant. Muslims seek Laylat al-Qadr through increased prayer, Quran recitation, and remembrance.

facts.title: Community Iftars
facts.content: Sharing Iftar with family, friends, or the needy is a beloved tradition. Many mosques and organizations host free community Iftars.

facts.title: Quran in Ramadan
facts.content: The Quran was revealed in Ramadan. Many Muslims aim to complete at least one full recitation (khatm) of the Quran during the month.

facts.title: Fasting and empathy
facts.content: Experiencing hunger and thirst helps build empathy for those who lack food and water. Ramadan often inspires increased charity and social justice efforts.

facts.title: Odd nights
facts.content: Laylat al-Qadr is often sought on the odd nights of the last ten: 21st, 23rd, 25th, 27th, or 29th. 'The Night of Power is better than a thousand months.'

facts.title: Final third
facts.content: The last third of Ramadan is a time of intensified worship and reflection. Many observe i'tikaf (seclusion in the mosque) in the last ten days.

facts.title: Night of Power
facts.content: One of the most likely nights for Laylat al-Qadr. Muslims spend the night in prayer, Quran recitation, and supplication.

facts.title: Sadaqat al-Fitr
facts.content: Before Eid prayer, Muslims give Sadaqat al-Fitr (charity of breaking the fast)—typically the value of one meal per person—so the needy can celebrate Eid.

facts.title: Another odd night
facts.content: Another highly regarded night for Laylat al-Qadr. Many stay awake in worship until dawn.

facts.title: Eid countdown
facts.content: Eid al-Fitr is announced after the new moon is sighted, marking the end of Ramadan. Celebrations include special prayer, new clothes, and feasting.

facts.title: Last odd night
facts.content: The 27th is widely observed as Laylat al-Qadr in many regions, but all odd nights of the last ten are valued.

facts.title: Reflection
facts.content: As Ramadan draws to a close, many reflect on the month's lessons: gratitude, discipline, and connection to the Divine.

facts.title: Laylat al-Qadr (27th)
facts.content: Many Muslims observe the 27th night as Laylat al-Qadr. Mosques are full for night prayers and Quran recitation.

facts.title: Last days
facts.content: The final days are a time to complete any missed fasts (if applicable) and increase good deeds before Eid.

facts.title: Moon sighting
facts.content: The end of Ramadan is confirmed by the sighting of the new moon. If sighted, the next day is Eid al-Fitr.

facts.title: Eid Mubarak
facts.content: After 30 days (or 29 if the moon was sighted), Muslims celebrate Eid al-Fitr—a day of gratitude, joy, and community.
